extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy (undergraduates, general educated readers, scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading / study of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (Book I): theory of the Chief Good (Happiness), the function argument, classification of lives and goods, and methodological remarks about moral/political inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief Good (that which all things aim at)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Good is 'that which all things aim at' — the one End which we desire for its own sake and with a view to which we desire everything else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle frames the object of ethics as the single final End of human action; this is the starting point for ethical inquiry and must be described, at least in outline, rather than proved with mathematical exactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality of Happiness (absolutely final)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is 'absolutely final' in that it is chosen always for its own sake and never with a view to some further thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the test of whether something is ever chosen as a means to something else; if it is never chosen for something else, it qualifies as a final good. Examples contrasted: honour, pleasure, intellect — these can be chosen both for themselves and as means to happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficiency of the final good
rubrics_metrics.description: The final good must be self-sufficient: 'which taken alone makes life choice-worthy, and to be in want of nothing'; self-sufficiency is judged not for a solitary individual only but in relation to family, friends, and citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating candidate ends, test whether possessing them alone makes life worthy and lacking nothing; consider social relations as part of the standard for self-sufficiency (parents, children, friends, countrymen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish independent (final) goods from instrumental goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods must be classified as those pursued for their own sakes (independent/final goods: e.g., wisdom, certain pleasures) and those pursued for the sake of other goods (instrumental goods: e.g., wealth as means).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether a candidate good is desired per se or as a means; the ethical account must separate independent goods from those valuable only because they conduce to other goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Function (Work) Argument for human good
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand the human good we should discover the 'work' or function of man: not mere life (shared with plants) nor sensation (shared with animals), but the life of the Rational Nature — activity of the rational part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate human excellence by asking what activity is distinctive of humans (rational activity) and then consider performing that activity well as constitutive of the good life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemplative life as highest form of Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle argues that the highest and most satisfying form of life is 'the contemplative life' — the life of philosophical/scientific contemplation — because it is the activity of the rational part at its best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing ways of life, assess the quality of the activity (intellectual/contemplative vs. practical), and favour the form that manifests the highest exercise of rationality; note Aristotle's caveats about accessibility and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as concomitant and index of perfect activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is 'the natural concomitant and index of perfect activity, distinguishable but inseparable from it' — always a good in itself, but its value rises and falls with the value of the activity it accompanies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assess pleasures in isolation; evaluate pleasures by the worth of the activity they accompany. Highest pleasures are those that accompany the highest activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor is not the ultimate good (dependence on others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Honour is an inadequate candidate for the Chief Good because it depends on the judgment of others ('it rests with those who pay rather than with him who receives it') and so cannot be the fully final good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject goods whose value is excessively external or contingent on others' opinions when seeking the Chief Good; prefer goods intrinsically owned by the agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate methodological exactness for ethics/politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactness must not be looked for in all discussions alike; ethical and political inquiries admit of variation and error and should be treated roughly and in outline when the subject-matter requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set expectations for rigor according to subject matter: do not demand demonstrative mathematical proof in moral/political discourse; provide reasonably general conclusions from general data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of the student of Moral Philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The young (in years or temperament) and those given to passion and following impulses are not fit students of Moral Philosophy because they lack life experience and are apt to hear 'as though he heard not'; those who form desires and act in accordance with reason profit from such study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider maturity of life experience and self-control as prerequisites for productive study of ethics; pedagogy and timing matter when teaching moral philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral action presupposes thought but requires situational knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Right action presupposes Thinking: not merely calculation of means to an end but 'thinking which reveals to the agent the situation' — knowledge of universal conditions and the particular, ever-varying situation in which the agent finds himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or prescribing moral action, prioritise practical wisdom (phronesis) that integrates general principles with concrete facts rather than mere rule-following or abstract calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political science aims at producing the best life via law
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of life in the state is well-living and well-doing; the State's great agency is Law (Reason backed by Force), and the best polity would embody the best reason in its laws — requiring a 'science of legislation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In political evaluation, assess whether laws and institutions embody communal reason and cultivate conditions for the best life; legislators must study general principles of law, morality, and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical value of abstract 'very-good' is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if there is a single abstract 'very-good' (the Platonic idea), it cannot be the practical object of human action; ethical inquiry should aim at concrete goods attainable by humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer actionable, concrete conceptions of good when advising or guiding conduct; abstract metaphysical formulations of 'good' may be useless for artisans or practical decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate goods by their category and relevant science
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'good' is predicated in many ways across categories (substance, quality, quantity, relation, time, place), account of goodness must be sensitive to the category in question and the corresponding practical science (e.g., medicine for health, generalship for seasonableness in war).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging goodness in a domain, use the standards and sciences appropriate to that category rather than a single universal criterion across disparate domains.
